newsitem.title: USA: Rawlings near deal on commerative baseballs.
newsitem.headline: Rawlings near deal on commerative baseballs.

text.p: ORLANDO, Jan 24, Reuter - Trying to counter a slump in its vital baseball markets, Rawlings Sporting Goods Inc said on Friday it is near signing deals to produce commerative baseballs marking the 1947 entry of Jackie Robinson into Major League Baseball and Joe DiMaggio's 56-game hitting streak as a New York Yankee.
"They're not finalized but we're confident the balls will be made," Rawlings chief financial officer Paul Martin said after a talk at an investors conference sponsored by AG Edwards & Sons.

Rawlings could sell 60,000 to 72,000 of each of the commerative ballls, with royalties likely to average 18 to 20 percent to Major League Baseball, team owners and DiMaggio or Robinson's estate, Martin said.
"They would probably mean $1.5 million to $2 million in incremental revenue (for Rawlings)," Martin said.

Martin said Robinson baseballs carrying the famous black player's name will be used in all opening Major League Baseball games in April. Half a century ago, Robinson was the first black athlete to compete in the major leagues when he took the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers.
The late player's debut marked a sea change in U.S. race relations.

DiMaggio, now in his 80s, scored a hit in 56 consecutive games during 1941, a streak which fascinated Americans and fixed the laconic athlete as a U.S. sports hero. The DiMaggio balls would likely be autographed by DiMaggio and would retail for about $500. The balls would be released midway through the 1997 baseball season, Martin said.
"He wants to do it this year," Martin said of DiMaggio.

Rawlings has already made and sold commerative baseballs for Carl Ripken Jr and the late Mickey Mantle, a New York Yankee who died last year before the team won the World Series. The Ripken ball, Martin told investors, had gross profit margins before payment of royalties of about 50 percent.

Synomous with baseball, Rawlings makes bats, balls and other equipment. Its baseball-related sales, accounting for about 60 percent of the company's $150 million in revenues, have drooped since the 1994 professional baseball strike. The company's operating profits were flat during the last two fiscal years, Martin said.
